title: The Pilgrim Road to the Moika: Pokrovskoye, Jerusalem, and the Watched Flat on Gorokhovaya
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Pokrovskoye, the birth entered in the register
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The Pokrovskoye parish baptismal register, transcribed and discussed by the Tyumen regional state archive, fixes the birth to 9 January 1869 Old Style; 21 January New Style follows the twelve-day nineteenth-century offset. Coordinates are the settlement centre of Pokrovskoye in Yarkovsky District, Tyumen Oblast (57.24506, 66.79375); an earlier pin in the research pool sat roughly sixty-seven kilometres north-northwest in empty taiga and is rejected. The exact house site is not independently geolocated.
stops.campa: A son is born to the state peasants Yefim and Anna Rasputin in Pokrovskoye, a village strung along the Tura on the cart road between Tyumen and Tobolsk. The house stands among houses like it. There is no wonder-child in the parish register, no comet, no visitation; there is a line of ink recording a birth in a governorate where most births are recorded and forgotten. Of roughly seven children born to this couple, three will live to be adults. He is one of the three.
suggested_refs: The Pokrovskoye parish baptismal register, Tobolsk governorate, entry of 9 January 1869 Old Style
sources: Tyumen regional state archive (archiv.72to.ru) and Tyumen Today (tumentoday.ru), 150th-anniversary account transcribing the register
Smithsonian Magazine, 'What Really Happened During the Murder of Rasputin'

stops.name: Pokrovskoye, the Church of the Intercession: the naming
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the fact and the custom, arithmetical as to the New Style date. The baptism took place the day after the birth, 10 January 1869 Old Style, and the name was taken from the church calendar, where the feast of Gregory of Nyssa falls that day. The New Style equivalent is derived by the same twelve-day offset applied to the birth, not supplied by a source. Coordinates are the village; the parish church building is not separately geolocated.
stops.campa: He is carried to the Church of the Intercession the day after he is born and baptized Grigori, for Gregory of Nyssa, whose feast falls on the tenth of January. The name is not chosen. Orthodox custom takes it from the calendar, so the boy receives a theologian of the Cappadocian fathers the way a farmer receives weather. Nobody in the church has read Gregory of Nyssa. The priest writes the name, the parents carry the child home, and the register closes on a page identical to the pages around it.
suggested_refs: The Church of the Intercession at Pokrovskoye, parish of his baptism and of his marriage

stops.name: Pokrovskoye, the carting road
stops.date_confidence: Inferred, for ordering only. No source dates his entry into carting work. The pattern of farm and carting labour on the Tyumen-Tobolsk road through his youth, and rudimentary adult literacy, are attested in the general biographical literature; the 1885 date is a placement. Childhood-visions and wonder-child stories reported elsewhere are legendary retrospection and are omitted rather than reported as fact.
stops.campa: He farms, carts freight, and drives passengers along the road that ties Tyumen to Tobolsk, so pilgrims, officials, exiles, priests and merchants pass through his village and sometimes through his cart. He learns to read late and badly and never learns to write a clean sentence; everything he later puts on paper, he dictates. What he learns instead is how strangers talk and how quickly a man who listens closely can seem to know things about them. He is on that road, in that work, through his twenties.
suggested_refs: The Tyumen to Tobolsk post road, running through Pokrovskoye
sources: Smithsonian Magazine, 'What Really Happened During the Murder of Rasputin'

stops.name: Abalak, the monastery festival
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction firming toward attested. The research pool records the meeting with Praskovya Fyodorovna Dubrovina at a pilgrimage or church festival near Abalak, dated 'probably 1886' by the dossier and 1886 outright by en.wikipedia. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinates corrected to the village of Abalak on the Irtysh (58.12972, 68.5975); the pool's earlier pin lay about seven and a half kilometres west of the monastery site.
stops.campa: At the Abalak monastery above the Irtysh, where the wonderworking icon of the Sign draws pilgrims from across the governorate, he meets Praskovya Fyodorovna Dubrovina, a peasant girl on pilgrimage as he is a peasant boy on pilgrimage. He is seventeen; she is a few years older. What passes between them at the festival nobody writes down, and the tradition that fixes the encounter here rests on the reconstruction of biographers rather than on a document. They marry the following February.
suggested_refs: The Abalak Znamensky Monastery on the Irtysh, near Tobolsk, and its festival of the icon of the Sign

stops.name: Pokrovskoye, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the standard biographies (Fuhrmann, Smith) and in en.wikipedia as February 1887; the verifier did not fetch a parish marriage register. Day unknown, defaulted to 01. Month is given Old Style in the sources and is left unconverted.
stops.campa: They marry in the Church of the Intercession, in February, in the village where he was baptized eighteen years earlier. Praskovya takes over the house and the ground and holds both through every absence that follows, and the absences run long: pilgrimages of months, then years in the capital, then a police guard on the door. She does not divorce him, does not denounce him, and does not appear in the Petrograd scandal at all. In 1930 she is dispossessed in the collectivization and deported north. What became of her after that is not documented in any source reached.
suggested_refs: Praskovya Fyodorovna Dubrovina, dispossessed in the collectivization of 1930 and deported north
sources: Research dossier chronology and genealogical section

stops.name: Pokrovskoye, the children
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the three surviving children: Dmitri 1895, Matryona 1898, Varvara 1900, of roughly seven born. Month and day of the anchor date unknown, defaulted to 01. Matryona's later career is well documented (en.wikipedia, 'Maria Rasputin': born 27 March 1898 Pokrovskoye, died 27 September 1977 Los Angeles; Busch Circus 1929, Hagenbeck-Wallace from 1935, a season as a lion tamer, mauled by a bear in May 1935, US citizen 1946, three memoirs) and the research pool's [R] tag on it is upgraded here. The 1930 dispossession and deportation of Praskovya and Dmitri remains [R], not confirmed against a Soviet-era record.
stops.campa: Dmitri is born in 1895, Matryona in 1898, Varvara in 1900. Around them are the other births, four or so, that do not survive infancy; the household buries roughly as many children as it keeps, which in a Tobolsk village in the 1890s passes without comment. Praskovya raises the three who live. Dmitri will be dispossessed and deported north in 1930 and die in that decade. Matryona will dance in Berlin cabarets and work an American circus. Varvara will follow her father to Petrograd and share the flat on Gorokhovaya Street.
suggested_refs: Maria Rasputin, The Real Rasputin (1929), Rasputin My Father (1932), and The Man Behind the Myth (1977)

stops.name: Verkhoturye, the Monastery of St Nicholas
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The extended pilgrimage to Verkhoturye around 1897 is standard in the biographical literature and in the research pool's chronology, but no primary source for it was fetched; the town coordinates are confirmed via en.wikipedia. His motive is explicitly disputed in the sources between religious crisis, grief, a vow, and flight from a village accusation, and is left open. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Ten years married and twenty-eight years old, he leaves Pokrovskoye on foot for the monastery of St Nicholas at Verkhoturye in the Urals, where the relics of St Simeon lie. Why he goes is the most contested fact of his early life: a religious crisis, a vow, grief, or a horse-theft accusation he wanted distance from. He gives no reason himself beyond the one he dictates a decade later, that he decided to become a pilgrim. He comes back after months with the vocabulary of a holy man and the habit of not eating meat.
stops.quote: First I lived like everyone else with my worldly interests and pleasures until I was 28 years of age.
stops.quote_source: Grigori Rasputin, Zhitie opytnogo strannika (The Life of an Experienced Pilgrim), c. 1907, English translation at omolenko.com
suggested_refs: The Monastery of St Nicholas at Verkhoturye and the relics of St Simeon of Verkhoturye
sources: Grigori Rasputin, The Life of an Experienced Pilgrim, c. 1907

stops.name: Aktai, the skete of the elder Makary
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The encounter with the elder Makary at the Aktai skete near Verkhoturye is reported consistently across the biographical literature but rests on retrospective testimony from both hostile and admiring camps; no primary document was reached. Coordinates are an approximate placement near Verkhoturye, not a landmark fix. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01; the stop shares its date with the Verkhoturye stop and follows it in the same pilgrimage.
stops.campa: In the forest skete at Aktai, a few hours from Verkhoturye, he finds the elder Makary. For the rest of his life, asked who taught him, he gives that name and no other. What Makary actually said to him is not recorded by anyone who heard it. The whole relation reaches us through Rasputin's own later account and through people with reasons to build him up or tear him down. Whether the hermit made the holy man, or the holy man afterwards made the hermit, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The Aktai skete near Verkhoturye, and the elder Makary, his most frequently cited spiritual influence
sources: Research dossier, which itself calls the documentation 'largely retrospective but consistent across camps'
Grigori Rasputin, The Life of an Experienced Pilgrim, c. 1907

stops.name: Kyiv, the caves of the Lavra
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The research pool lists Kyiv among the repeated pilgrimages of his formation years, reconstructed from later biography rather than from a dated itinerary; no fetched source places him there on a specific date. Coordinates for the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra are confirmed via en.wikipedia. Year approximate, month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He walks to Kyiv, as tens of thousands of Russian peasants walk to Kyiv, and goes down into the caves of the Lavra where the mummified monks lie in their niches. The pilgrim road is the one institution of the empire a Tobolsk peasant can enter on the same terms as a countess, and he uses it for years: Abalak, Verkhoturye, Kyiv, and further. He begs his bread, sleeps in monastery yards, and is fed by people for whom feeding a strannik on the road is a duty laid on them by God.
stops.quote: This does not belong to me. These all are God's possessions. Take whatever you want.
stops.quote_source: Grigori Rasputin, The Life of an Experienced Pilgrim, c. 1907, English translation at omolenko.com, addressing robbers met on the pilgrim road
suggested_refs: The near and far caves of the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, terminus of the great Russian pilgrim road
sources: Grigori Rasputin, The Life of an Experienced Pilgrim

stops.name: Mount Athos, the Russian monastery of St Panteleimon
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the weakest-attested journey in this file. Some biographies report an Athos pilgrimage; the date is variously given as around 1900, 1903, or later, and no independent primary source was located. Coordinates corrected to the Russian monastery of St Panteleimon (40.23694, 24.20194); the pool's earlier longitude placed the pin some seven kilometres out to sea. Year, month and day are a placement within the pilgrimage segment, not a finding.
stops.campa: The Russian house on the Holy Mountain, St Panteleimon, holds thousands of monks from the empire in these years and takes in Russian pilgrims off the boats at Daphne, most of them peasants who crossed the Black Sea on subsidised fares. Whether Rasputin is among them is the least secure claim in his biography. Some accounts put him on Athos and date the journey to 1900, or to 1903, or later; others leave it out entirely. No document has been produced on either side, and no source reached here settles it.
suggested_refs: The Russian Monastery of St Panteleimon on Mount Athos, and the Odessa to Daphne pilgrim steamers
sources: Research dossier, hedged account, no primary source located

stops.name: Kazan, the patrons of the theological academy
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The research pool reports clerical and upper-class patronage acquired at Kazan around 1903 to 1905, sourced to the dossier rather than to a fetched document; the Kazan Theological Academy coordinates are corrected to 55.792, 49.151, about nine kilometres southeast of the pool's earlier pin. The year of his first move west is itself disputed among 1903, 1904 and 1905. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: In Kazan he is passed upward. Priests and devout gentlewomen who meet the Siberian pilgrim decide he is worth an introduction, and introductions in the Russian church are a currency; a letter from a Kazan cleric opens a door at the Petersburg Theological Academy. Nothing in his manner changes. He wears the same coat, speaks the same dialect, and is recommended precisely because he does. What year he first goes west is not settled: 1903, 1904 and 1905 all appear in the literature, and no source chooses between them.
suggested_refs: The Kazan Theological Academy and its circle of clerical patrons
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Kazan Theological Academy' and ru.wikipedia for coordinates
Research dossier chronology, disputed as to year

stops.name: St Petersburg, the first arrival
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, date disputed and not resolved. The research pool records the first journey to the capital as variously dated 1903, 1904, and the winter of 1904 to 1905, with no source settling it; 1904-01-01 is a placement. Coordinates are a central St Petersburg pin standing for the city at large rather than a lodging address, which is not known.
stops.campa: He arrives in the capital with letters of introduction, a beard, and no money, and is put up in church lodgings. The city he enters is a year from revolution and its drawing rooms are full of people looking for what the official church is not giving them: spiritualists, table-rappers, French mystics with fabricated titles, a whole market in holiness that the war with Japan and the strikes will widen further. Into it walks a man who has actually walked to Kyiv. He is thirty-five and carries a change of shirt.
suggested_refs: The Petersburg salon culture of mystics and healers in the years before 1905
sources: Research dossier chronology, tagged as tradition and reconstruction

stops.name: St Petersburg, the Theological Academy and Archimandrite Feofan
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, site inferred. Feofan (Bystrov), inspector and later rector of the St Petersburg Theological Academy, is well established as an early clerical patron who broke with him around 1910 and said so publicly, but no primary source placing specific meetings at this address was reached; the coordinates are the Alexander Nevsky Lavra and academy district. Year approximate, month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Archimandrite Feofan, inspector of the Theological Academy and a confessor to the imperial family, takes him up. Feofan is a serious ascetic with a scholar's training and believes he has found the real thing: a man of prayer produced by the Russian countryside rather than by a seminary. He introduces him to the Montenegrin grand duchesses Militsa and Anastasia, who collect mystics. Around 1910 Feofan will conclude he was wrong, say so publicly, and be moved out of the capital for saying it.
suggested_refs: The St Petersburg Theological Academy and the Alexander Nevsky Lavra district
sources: Research dossier account of Feofan's patronage and rupture

stops.name: Sergievka, Old Peterhof: tea with Militsa and Stana
stops.date_confidence: Attested, with a contradiction inside the research pool flagged rather than resolved. Nicholas II's diary for 1 November 1905 Old Style, 14 November New Style, records the meeting. Ru.wikipedia locates it at Sergievka, the Leuchtenberg estate at Old Peterhof where the imperial couple took tea with Militsa and Anastasia Nikolaevna; en.wikipedia says 'the Peterhof Palace'; the pool's own geography lens placed the same event at the Alexander Palace, Tsarskoye Selo. Coordinates follow the Sergievka reading (approximately 59.881, 29.863). The diary text is verified via ru.wikipedia and Douglas Smith, Rasputin (2016), p. 65; the verifier could not open the Tyumen archival page originally cited.
stops.campa: At four in the afternoon the Tsar and Tsaritsa drive the short distance to Sergievka and take tea with the Montenegrin sisters, Militsa and Stana, who have a Siberian to show them. The empire is nine months past Bloody Sunday and six weeks past the October Manifesto, and the man who signed it under duress spends the afternoon at a relative's estate meeting a peasant pilgrim. Nicholas writes the encounter down that evening in the flat, incurious hand he uses for weather and for shooting bags. The entry is one sentence long.
stops.quote: We became acquainted with a man of God - Gregory from Tobolsk province.
stops.quote_source: Diary of Nicholas II, entry of 1 November 1905 Old Style; Russian text at ru.wikipedia, English rendering compare Douglas Smith, Rasputin (2016), p. 65
suggested_refs: Sergievka, the Leuchtenberg estate at Old Peterhof, where Militsa Nikolaevna received him

stops.name: Tsarskoye Selo, the Alexander Palace: the children
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the meetings, Old Style as to the date. The research pool records presentations to the imperial couple on 18 July and again in October 1906, the July occasion being the first at which he meets the imperial children; the source gives Old Style without a New Style equivalent, so the date stands as printed and the thirteen-day conversion is left unapplied. The icon of St Simeon of Verkhoturye he is reported to have brought is attested in the Smithsonian's biographical account.
stops.campa: He is brought to the Alexander Palace and this time the children are present: four grand duchesses and a boy not yet two whose navel would not stop bleeding when he was born. He carries with him an icon of St Simeon of Verkhoturye, the saint of the Urals monastery where his own pilgrimages began. The Tsaritsa has been waiting for a sign that God has not abandoned her son, and here is a peasant come from Siberia holding a piece of the country's own holiness. He gives them the icon, asks for nothing, and is brought back to the palace again in October.
suggested_refs: The icon of St Simeon of Verkhoturye, carried from the Urals to the imperial family
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Grigori Rasputin', chronology of the 1906 meetings
Smithsonian Magazine, 'What Really Happened During the Murder of Rasputin'
Pierre Gilliard, memoir of the Tsarskoye Selo court, alexanderpalace.org

stops.name: Tsarskoye Selo, the illness in the heir
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The episode in which Alexandra turns to Rasputin's prayers during a bleeding crisis is commonly dated to 1907 across popular and academic biographies, but no single primary document fixes it, and the research pool tags it [R]. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Separately attested is the pattern of recurring informal audiences at Tsarskoye Selo from 1906 to 1916, and that he performed no documented medical procedure and was never the boy's physician.
stops.campa: Alexei bleeds. Haemophilia in 1907 has no treatment; the doctors can only stand beside a child screaming as blood fills a joint, and the Tsaritsa has been told by physicians that nothing can be done. Rasputin prays, speaks quietly, and tells her the boy will live. The boy lives. Whether the calm he brings into the room slows the bleeding, whether the crises were self-limiting, whether the aspirin the doctors gave was making things worse: the record does not settle it. Alexandra settles it. She believes God sent him.
suggested_refs: The haemophilia of Tsarevich Alexei and the medical practice of 1907
sources: Research dossier, tagged as tradition and reconstruction, no primary document
Pierre Gilliard, memoir of the Tsarskoye Selo court, alexanderpalace.org

stops.name: Pokrovskoye, dictating The Life of an Experienced Pilgrim
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The text dates itself internally to May 1907. It is dictated: his literacy was rudimentary, and the surviving prose was taken down and tidied by literate followers, which the research pool treats as leaving the work substantially authentic rather than ghostwritten. Day unknown, defaulted to 01. The hosting site, omolenko.com, names neither translator nor translation date, a gap worth flagging.
stops.campa: He dictates his account of the pilgrim years to somebody who can write, and it comes out in short, jolting, ungrammatical paragraphs that no editor entirely smooths. One passage is about robbers on the road, whom he tells that the goods are not his but God's and they may take what they want. Another names a happiness he calls the chains of love. Nothing in it touches hierarchy or doctrine, and the Khlysty are never mentioned; the pages are full of walking, weather, and other people's faces. The text dates itself to May 1907.
stops.quote: I found the chains of love. I loved everyone. I would see people leaving the temple and would love them.
stops.quote_source: Grigori Rasputin, The Life of an Experienced Pilgrim, c. 1907, English translation at omolenko.com
suggested_refs: Zhitie opytnogo strannika (The Life of an Experienced Pilgrim), dictated May 1907
sources: Grigori Rasputin, The Life of an Experienced Pilgrim, Russian and English texts at omolenko.com

stops.name: Tobolsk, the consistory opens the Khlyst file
stops.date_confidence: Attested, Old Style as printed. Ru.wikipedia records the Tobolsk consistory case opened on 6 September 1907 on the basis of a denunciation lodged in 1903; the source gives Old Style without a New Style equivalent and the date stands unconverted. The substance of the file rests on the research pool's synthesis of the diocesan record and on the Orthodox Life article on the canonization debate, which the verifier did not fetch directly. Coordinates confirmed for Tobolsk via en.wikipedia.
stops.campa: The diocese opens a case. The charge is that he belongs to the Khlysty, the banned ecstatic sect whose rites were said to mix flagellation, dancing and sex, and the charge comes up from his own village, from neighbours who have watched him hold prayer meetings in his cellar with women present. Under Russian law sectarian membership is a crime with a real penalty attached. The file will run twenty months. It is opened on the strength of a denunciation lodged four years earlier and left in a drawer.
suggested_refs: The Tobolsk diocesan consistory file on the Khlyst allegation, opened 1907
sources: Orthodox Life, 'The Real Rasputin' (cited in the dossier, not fetched by the verifier)

stops.name: Tobolsk, the bishop closes the file
stops.date_confidence: Attested, Old Style as printed, per ru.wikipedia: the consistory case closed on 7 May 1908 with the bishop declaring him a Christian man spiritually disposed and seeking the truth of Christ. The New Style equivalent would be 20 May 1908; the source gives Old Style and it is left unconverted. The acquittal is the load-bearing half of the episode and is frequently omitted in later polemic. The 1912 reopening after Novoselov's pamphlet is documented in the pool's chronology as [R].
stops.campa: The consistory closes the case and the bishop's finding is entered: a Christian man, spiritually disposed and seeking the truth of Christ. No conviction, no penance, no bar to communion. The polemicists of the next decade will cite the investigation constantly and the acquittal almost never, and in 1912, when Novoselov publishes his pamphlet on mystical debauchery and the press campaign opens, the file will be reopened. It ends the same way. Nobody proves he is a Khlyst, and nobody stops saying it.
suggested_refs: Mikhail Novoselov, Grigory Rasputin and Mystical Debauchery (1912), confiscated on publication
sources: Research dossier chronology for the 1912 reopening

segments.name: The Holy Land and the Break with the Church

stops.name: St Petersburg, the house on the Winter Canal
stops.date_confidence: Attested from a single hostile source. Felix Yusupov's memoir Lost Splendor, chapter XV, describes the first meeting at an aristocratic house on the Winter Canal at Christmas 1909; the source does not state which calendar its Christmas belongs to and the date is left as printed. The testimony is the eventual murderer's, written decades afterwards, and is treated as evidence that the encounter happened rather than as neutral description of Rasputin's conduct.
stops.campa: At a house on the Winter Canal, twenty-two-year-old Prince Felix Yusupov, heir to the largest private fortune in Russia, is introduced to the peasant everyone is talking about. Rasputin moves to embrace him. Yusupov recoils. Seven years separate this room from the basement on the Moika, and the only witness who ever described either scene is the man who did the shooting, writing decades afterwards and in print. In his telling, Rasputin looks at him and says he will go far, very far.
suggested_refs: Felix Yusupov, Lost Splendor, chapter XV, the first meeting
sources: Felix Yusupov, Lost Splendor, ch. XV, alexanderpalace.org/lostsplendor/XV.html

stops.name: Odessa, taking ship for the Holy Land
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to place and date. The 1911 pilgrimage to Ottoman Jerusalem is attested and analysed in Rachel Mairs's academic study of his pilgrimage writing, which the verifier could not fetch (the University of Reading repository and the journal both returned bot-protection blocks). The Black Sea crossing appears in his own dictated book, but no source names the port of embarkation; Odessa was the standard departure for Russian pilgrims to Jaffa, and these coordinates are not supplied by the research pool. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Russian pilgrims for Jerusalem go by steamer from the Black Sea to Jaffa, packed in deck class by the thousand, an operation the Imperial Orthodox Palestine Society runs at subsidised fares so that peasants can afford it. He goes with them, as a pilgrim rather than as the court favourite the newspapers already call him. The sea is new to a Siberian, and he dictates afterwards that it soothes the soul, that you get up in the morning and the waves are talking. No source names the port he sailed from; Odessa is where Russian pilgrims for Jaffa normally embarked. It is the only time he leaves the empire.
stops.quote: The sea soothes the soul easily. You get up in the morning and the waves are talking and splashing making you happy.
stops.quote_source: Grigori Rasputin, Moi mysli i razmyshleniya (My Thoughts and Reflections), Petrograd, 1915, English translation at omolenko.com
suggested_refs: The Imperial Orthodox Palestine Society's subsidised pilgrim steamers from Odessa to Jaffa
sources: Grigori Rasputin, My Thoughts and Reflections (1915), omolenko.com
Rachel Mairs, study of Rasputin's pilgrimage writing, Taylor & Francis 2023 (not reachable to the verifier)

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the pilgrimage and the book that came out of it, approximate as to date. The documentary basis is Rachel Mairs's study, which the verifier could not open directly; the pilgrimage itself is well attested across the biographical literature. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the standing Jerusalem pin inherited byte-identical from the interlock lens, rather than the church's own footprint at 31.7783, 35.2297.
stops.campa: He comes into the rotunda where the stone is, in the press of Russian and Greek and Armenian pilgrims who have crossed a sea to stand there. What he dictates afterwards is neither doctrine nor scandal; it is a man saying that he did not want to leave the place. The book carrying it is printed in Petrograd in 1915, while the newspapers are calling him a German agent and a drunk; the same year, the same man, publishes several thousand words about Jerusalem and how quiet it made him. The pilgrimage itself is attested across the literature. What he did on any given day in the city is recorded nowhere.
stops.quote: Paradise on earth, do not disappear, stay with me and be in me!
stops.quote_source: Grigori Rasputin, My Thoughts and Reflections, Petrograd, 1915, English translation at omolenko.com
suggested_refs: Moi mysli i razmyshleniya (My Thoughts and Reflections), Petrograd: V. D. Smirnov press, 1915
sources: Grigori Rasputin, My Thoughts and Reflections (1915), omolenko.com

stops.name: St Petersburg, Vasilyevsky Island: the crucifix
stops.date_confidence: Attested in outline, contested in detail, Old Style month as printed. En.wikipedia's article on Hermogenes (Dolganyov) places the December 1911 assault in a monastery on Vasilyevsky Island; the research pool's geography lens had put it in the central Nevsky Prospekt area, about four kilometres east, and that placement is rejected here. Coordinates are an approximate Vasilyevsky Island placement, not a confirmed address. All accounts are partisan memoir. A castration detail that appears in later retellings is unverified and omitted. Day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Bishop Hermogenes and the monk Iliodor, who had both promoted him, summon him to a monastery on Vasilyevsky Island and demand that he renounce the court and leave the capital. Hermogenes strikes him with a crucifix. He gets out, goes to the imperial couple, and within weeks Hermogenes and the holy fool Mitya Kozelsky are expelled to the Zhyrovichy monastery without trial. Iliodor leaves the church altogether and begins assembling the material that will send a knife to Pokrovskoye in 1914.
suggested_refs: Iliodor (Sergei Trufanov), The Mad Monk of Russia, the campaign of a former patron
sources: Research dossier synthesis of the partisan memoir accounts

stops.name: Spala, the telegram to the dying boy
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the crisis and the telegram's arrival, Old Style date as printed, reconstruction as to the wording. The Alexander Palace Time Machine account of the Spala crisis records the doctors giving Alexei almost no chance on 6 October 1912 and the reply telegraphed to Anna Vyrubova. The wording is rendered from General Spiridovich's French memoir of 1929, not from a located original telegram, and the research pool tags the quotation [R]. Coordinates for Spala in Russian Poland are village-level and are not supplied by the research pool.
stops.campa: The court is at the hunting lodge at Spala in Russian Poland when the boy tears something internally and haemorrhages into his groin and thigh. He screams for days; the leg draws up; on the sixth of October the doctors tell the parents there is nothing left to try, and the court circular begins preparing the empire for the death of the heir. Anna Vyrubova telegraphs Siberia. Rasputin telegraphs back that the illness will not be dangerous and the doctors should not tire him. The bleeding stops.
stops.quote: The illness will not be dangerous. Do not let the doctors make him tired.
stops.quote_source: Rasputin's telegram to Anna Vyrubova, October 1912, as rendered from General Alexander Spiridovich, Les Dernieres Annees de la Cour de Tzarskoe Selo (Paris, 1929); no original telegram located
suggested_refs: The imperial hunting lodge at Spala, Russian Poland, and the 1912 crisis of the heir
sources: Alexander Palace Time Machine, 'Tsarevich Alexei's 1912 Spala Crisis'
Alexander Spiridovich, Les Dernieres Annees de la Cour de Tzarskoe Selo (1929)

stops.name: Petrograd, apartment 20 at 64 Gorokhovaya Street
stops.date_confidence: Attested in outline, tagged [R] in the research pool for the tenancy date of May 1914, which comes from the apartment museum's own account and from standard biographical chronology. Coordinates are OpenStreetMap's resolution of 64 Gorokhovaya (59.92320, 30.33097), replacing a pool pin about a kilometre northwest; number 64 stands at the Fontanka and Semyonovsky Bridge end of the street, not near the Sadovaya crossing as the pool's note reasoned. Day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He takes a flat on Gorokhovaya Street and his daughters Matryona and Varvara come from Siberia to live in it. The staircase fills from early morning: petitioners with requests for jobs, pardons, exemptions and transfers, women with letters, priests wanting bishoprics, speculators wanting contracts, and, on the corner in the cold, the police agents assigned to write down who goes up. The flat is the whole of his political machine. There is no office and no secretary; there is a telephone in the hall and a queue on the stairs.
suggested_refs: Apartment 20, 64 Gorokhovaya Street, Petrograd, his urban base from May 1914

stops.name: Pokrovskoye, the knife
stops.date_confidence: Attested. En.wikipedia dates the attack to 29 June Old Style, 12 July 1914 New Style, outside his home in Pokrovskoye, and gives Khionia Guseva's age as thirty-three. The verifier could not fetch the British Newspaper Archive account originally cited by the dossier (HTTP 403 at the original and redirected URLs). Coordinates corrected to the village's true position (57.24506, 66.79375).
stops.campa: He is home in the village, walking out from his gate, when a woman with her face wrapped comes up to him for alms and drives a knife into his stomach. Khionia Guseva is thirty-three and comes out of Iliodor's circle. She shouts that she has killed the Antichrist. He runs holding his intestines; she comes after him; he picks up a shaft from the ground and knocks her down, and the villagers take her. It is the twelfth of July 1914, a fortnight after Sarajevo. Guseva is found insane and confined rather than tried.
suggested_refs: Khionia Guseva, of Iliodor's circle, found insane and confined rather than tried
sources: Research dossier account; British Newspaper Archive source unreachable (HTTP 403)

stops.name: Tyumen, the hospital
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to surgery and prolonged recovery at Tyumen; the specific hospital building is identified in no source reached, and coordinates are city-level. The telegrams begging Nicholas II not to enter the war are tagged [R] in the research pool: the antiwar position is consistent across accounts, the wording varies by edition, and no verified original telegram was located. The 20 July date orders the segment and is not a documented arrival date. The quotation below was recorded a year later at Petrograd, not here, and the pool's citation of it to 20 June 1915 is corrected to 20 July 1915 on two fetch passes.
stops.campa: They operate at Tyumen and he lies there for weeks while Europe mobilises. From the bed he telegraphs the Tsar against the war, repeatedly, in the terms he uses for everything: that it will drown Russia in blood and finish the dynasty. Whether the telegrams read as they are printed in later memoirs cannot be checked, because the originals have not been produced. A year afterwards a police agent in Petrograd writes down what he says about that summer, and the position has not moved.
stops.quote: Last year, when I was lying in hospital, rumours were beginning to spread of the coming war; I begged the Tsar not to fight.
stops.quote_source: Rasputin, recorded by an Okhrana agent at Petrograd under the entry of 20 July 1915, translated surveillance journal at alexanderpalace.org
suggested_refs: The wartime recoding of his antiwar statements into the charge of being a German agent, traced in the archival study at aurora-journals.com
sources: Research dossier, telegram texts secondhand across biographies
aurora-journals.com, archival study of the 'traitor' image

stops.name: Moscow, the Yar
stops.date_confidence: Contested; tagged [R] in the research pool. A police report of 26 March 1915 Old Style describes a drunken scene at the Yar. Witnesses later recanted and some writers call the affair embellished or manufactured. The narrative rests on the Leiberov and Margolis article reproducing the police material, which the verifier did not fetch; the restaurant's own history page confirms only that Rasputin was a documented patron, and ru.wikipedia's Yar article, which covers the older Kuznetsky Most establishment, contains nothing on any 1915 scandal. Coordinates are OpenStreetMap's fix for the 1910 Yar building at 32/2 Leningradsky Prospekt (55.7848, 37.5694); in 1915 the address was the Petersburg Highway, Leningradsky Prospekt not existing until 1924.
stops.campa: The Yar is Moscow's great gypsy restaurant, out past the Petrovsky park, where merchants ruin themselves to choirs at four in the morning. What the police report says happened there is that Rasputin got drunk in a private room, exposed himself, told the singers he had the empress, and fought the staff. Dzhunkovsky, deputy minister of the interior, carries the report to the Tsar and loses his post over it. Witnesses afterwards take their statements back. The report is real. Whether the night was, the record does not settle.
suggested_refs: Leiberov and Margolis, on the Yar police dossier, russianway.rhga.ru
sources: Leiberov and Margolis, police material (not fetched by the verifier)
yar-restoran.ru, restaurant history page confirming his patronage
Research dossier, which calls it a contested police dossier rather than a transcript

stops.name: Tsarskoye Selo, the Tsar leaves for Stavka
stops.date_confidence: Attested, with the research pool's month corrected. Nicholas II assumed supreme command on 23 August 1915 Old Style, 5 September New Style; the pool's imprecise '1915-09' is replaced by the New Style date. The correspondence in which Alexandra relays 'Our Friend's' advice is published in the Alexander Palace Time Machine letters archive, which the pool cited without the verifier re-fetching each page, a gap worth closing if exact wording matters.
stops.campa: Nicholas takes personal command of the army and moves to headquarters at Mogilev, leaving his wife to run the interior of a country at war. She writes to him almost daily, and the letters carry Rasputin's opinions into the machinery of government: this minister and not that one, this bishop, this pardon, this grain shipment. In the fourteen months that follow, Russia changes prime minister four times and minister of the interior five times. How much of that is his doing has been argued over ever since. The same letters show the Tsar refusing as often as agreeing.
suggested_refs: The Alexandra to Nicholas correspondence, 1915-1916, alexanderpalace.org/letters
sources: Alexander Palace Time Machine imperial letters archive
ru.wikipedia and standard historiography for the 23 August Old Style assumption of command

stops.name: Petrograd, the surveillance journal opens
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The translated Okhrana surveillance journal at alexanderpalace.org begins on 1 January 1915 and runs to 10 February 1916. Its dates carry no stated calendar; Russian police records of these years are normally Old Style, in which case the New Style equivalents fall thirteen days later. The question is not resolved here, and all dates from this journal stand exactly as printed in the source.
stops.campa: From the first of January agents are posted on the staircase and in the street, and they write down everything: who comes, at what hour, how drunk he is, what he says on the telephone, what he charges. The file is not a moral indictment. It is a bureaucratic ledger, and it is the densest single source on how he actually spent a day: the singing, the bathhouse, the women, the priests, the telegrams to Tsarskoye Selo. The same men who write the reports are also his bodyguard.
suggested_refs: The Okhrana surveillance journal on Rasputin, 1 January 1915 to 10 February 1916

stops.name: Petrograd, the price of a pardon
stops.date_confidence: Attested from the Okhrana journal, entry of 12 January 1915: petitioners charged 250 roubles each to obtain pardons from the Tsar, one case a sect conviction and another a forgery conviction. Calendar unstated in the source, date as printed. That the money did not accumulate is a reading of the same file's pattern of disbursement rather than an accounting record, and is offered as such.
stops.campa: The agents record the tariff. Two hundred and fifty roubles a head, paid by petitioners, and in exchange he asks the Tsar for a pardon: one man convicted for belonging to a sect, another for forgery. He does not keep the money long. It goes out again to other petitioners, to drink, to the poor of his own village, to whoever is standing in the flat when it arrives. The traffic is real and the file proves it. That the money never accumulated is a reading of the file's pattern of payments rather than an accounting record, and no accounting record exists.
suggested_refs: The 250-rouble pardon fee recorded in the surveillance file, 12 January 1915

stops.name: Petrograd, the quarrel with his father
stops.date_confidence: Attested from the Okhrana journal, entry of 9 September 1915: a violent confrontation between Rasputin and his elderly father, bruises, bystanders separating them. Calendar unstated in the source, date as printed. Nothing further about the episode appears in any source reached.
stops.campa: Yefim Rasputin, who is old, has come from Pokrovskoye to Petrograd, and on the ninth of September the agents write down that father and son come to blows in the street, that bystanders pull them apart, and that there are bruises. The cause is not recorded, nor who struck first, nor whether they spoke again afterwards. It is one line in a police ledger, sitting between an entry about a visitor and an entry about a telephone call. No other source anywhere returns to it.
suggested_refs: Yefim Rasputin, the father, in Petrograd in 1915

stops.name: Petrograd, Villa Rode and the restaurants of the file
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the venues, approximate as to coordinates. The Okhrana journal names Villa Rode and Restaurant Donon among his regular haunts, with Donon entries on 8 December 1915 and 29 January 1916. The pin is Villa Rode on Kamennoostrovsky Prospekt, an approximate placement the fetched source does not confirm, since it names the venue and not an address; Donon stood at Moika embankment 24 near the Winter Canal, roughly 59.940, 30.321, and the research pool's earlier Donon pin lay about a kilometre too far east. Dates as printed, calendar unstated.
stops.campa: Villa Rode out on the islands, with its gypsy choir and its private rooms; Donon on the Moika, where the ministers eat. He is in both, and the agents follow him into both and write down the hours. Everyone concerned knows the file is being kept, including him, and it changes nothing about how he spends a night. He drinks Madeira by the bottle. One morning in January the agents record him coming home at seven o'clock, completely overcome with drink, in exactly those words.
suggested_refs: Villa Rode and Restaurant Donon, Petrograd, named in the surveillance file

stops.name: Petrograd, the telegram to Vyrubova
stops.date_confidence: Attested, with the research pool's citation corrected. The telegram is recorded under the entry of 13 January 1916 in the translated Okhrana journal, not 10 January 1915 as the pool first had it; the report begins on 1 January 1915 and contains no 10 January 1915 entry at all. Calendar unstated in the source, date as printed.
stops.campa: He telegraphs Tsarskoye Selo, addressed to Vyrubova, and the police copy the text out before it goes. The Russian is oracular and slightly broken. From the words alone it is not clear whom he means by his children, or what truth has not yet come. This is how he talks when he is being holy: not doctrine but an assured fog the receiver fills in herself. The copy goes into the surveillance file and the original goes on to the palace. Whether Alexandra read it as prophecy or as comfort, nobody wrote down.
stops.quote: God Himself keeps him in heavenly joy. Let the truth shine upon my children unto eternity; the time has not yet come to see clearly.
stops.quote_source: Rasputin, telegram to Anna Vyrubova, recorded in the Okhrana surveillance journal under 13 January 1916, alexanderpalace.org
suggested_refs: Anna Vyrubova, the Tsaritsa's confidante and the channel between the flat and the palace

stops.name: Petrograd, the agents told off
stops.date_confidence: Attested from the Okhrana journal, entry of 14 January 1916; calendar unstated in the source, date as printed. The same entry records him returning home at seven in the morning completely overcome with drink, which is quoted at the restaurants stop above.
stops.campa: He knows the men on the stairs by sight, and on the fourteenth of January he turns and tells them that one of them has been repeating that he held a lady on his knees, and that this is unseemly talk. The agent writes the rebuke into the very report he is being rebuked about. He is not trying to escape the surveillance; he is negotiating with it the way he negotiates with everything, face to face and in the plainest words available, with no visible sense that the arrangement is unusual. Then he goes up the stairs to the flat.
stops.quote: One of you has told someone that I held a lady on my knees. That is unseemly talk.
stops.quote_source: Rasputin to the agents watching him, Okhrana surveillance journal, entry of 14 January 1916, alexanderpalace.org
suggested_refs: The Okhrana agents assigned to 64 Gorokhovaya, simultaneously watching and guarding him

stops.name: Petrograd, now there will be an inquiry
stops.date_confidence: Attested from the Okhrana journal, entry of 9 February 1916; calendar unstated in the source, date as printed. The journal itself ends on 10 February 1916, which is why the last ten months of his life are documented far more thinly than the preceding thirteen.
stops.campa: On the ninth of February he says that it is a pity there has been so much talk, and that now there will be an inquiry. The agents write it down, as they write down everything else that week. The journal stops the day after next, on the tenth of February 1916, and nothing in the record replaces it; what he did with the last ten months of his life is known in far less detail than what he did with the thirteen months before them. He is forty-seven years old and has ten months to live.
stops.quote: It is a pity that there has been so much talk; now there will be an inquiry.
stops.quote_source: Rasputin, Okhrana surveillance journal, entry of 9 February 1916, alexanderpalace.org
suggested_refs: The closing entry of the surveillance journal, 10 February 1916

stops.name: Petrograd, 64 Gorokhovaya: named from the Duma tribune
stops.date_confidence: Attested, Old Style as printed. Pavel Milyukov delivered the 'Stupidity or Treason?' speech in the State Duma on 1 November 1916 Old Style, invoking the dark forces around the throne; the dating is consistent across the standard historiography. The stop is pinned at Rasputin's own flat, not at the Tauride Palace, because he was not present at the speech. The letters in which Nicholas II tells Alexandra that ministers are his to choose and asks her not to drag 'our Friend' into it are in the Alexander Palace Time Machine's November 1916 letters.
stops.campa: From the tribune of the Duma, Milyukov asks whether what is being done to Russia is stupidity or treason, and every man in the chamber knows which household is meant. The speech is banned and circulates in tens of thousands of typed copies. At headquarters Nicholas writes to his wife that the ministers are his to choose and asks her not to drag our Friend into this, which is evidence of a limit on the influence and also evidence that the limit had to be stated in writing. On Gorokhovaya the staircase is still full.
suggested_refs: Pavel Milyukov's 'Stupidity or Treason?' speech, State Duma, 1 November 1916 Old Style
sources: Alexander Palace Time Machine, November 1916 imperial letters
Standard historiography of the fall of the Romanovs, corroborated in the research dossier chronology

stops.name: Petrograd, leaving Gorokhovaya with Yusupov
stops.date_confidence: Attested, with the research pool's calendar collision resolved in favour of New Style throughout this segment. The departure is the night of 16 to 17 December 1916 Old Style, 29 to 30 December New Style; the pool carried the Old Style date for the departure and the New Style date for the killing, which put the same night two weeks apart. The sole narrative source for the evening is Yusupov's Lost Splendor, chapter XXIII, the murderer's own account. Details of his dress that night circulate widely in the biographical literature and are not independently verified here.
stops.campa: Yusupov comes for him at the flat, late, in a car with the curtains drawn, and the pretext is that Princess Irina wants to meet him. Irina is in the Crimea. He has been warned by the police, by his daughters, and by his own repeated presentiments, and he goes anyway. The agent on the staircase does not follow the car. Everything after this point in the night is known only from the accounts of the men who killed him, and they had eight years and a book contract in which to arrange it.
stops.quote: I'm protected against ill fortune...Disaster will come to anyone who lifts a finger against me.
stops.quote_source: Rasputin, as reported in Prince Felix Yusupov, Lost Splendor, ch. XXIII; the murderer's testimony, not an independently attested transcript
suggested_refs: Felix Yusupov, Lost Splendor, chapter XXIII, 'The Murder of Rasputin'
sources: Felix Yusupov, Lost Splendor, ch. XXIII, alexanderpalace.org/lostsplendor/XXIII.html

stops.name: Petrograd, the basement dining room of the Moika Palace
stops.date_confidence: The killing is attested; the sequence is not. Yusupov's Lost Splendor narrates poisoned cakes and wine with no effect, a shot indoors, a revival, pursuit into the courtyard, and further shots by Purishkevich. Roger Byard's forensic reassessment (Forensic Science, Medicine and Pathology, February 2024) finds a contact gunshot wound to the mid forehead with a muzzle imprint abrasion on the lower and right margins, no stippling, and no trace of poison, plus further lethal wounds to the liver and the kidney. The original autopsy report does not survive: Byard reasons from Kossorotov's documented findings, Zharov's 1993 review, and the postmortem photographs, so no surviving autopsy record can be quoted directly. Byard also notes that Rasputin avoided sweet food out of superstition. Coordinates are the Moika Palace at 59.9294, 30.2989; a pool pin at 59.928, 30.2939 sat about three hundred metres off and is rejected.
stops.campa: The room downstairs has been furnished for the evening: rugs, a fire, a cabinet of inlaid ivory, a table of cakes and Madeira. He drinks the wine. He eats, or does not eat, the cakes, which he had a lifelong superstition against. Then he is shot. Everything the story is famous for happens in the hour before that, and all of it comes from Yusupov: a man asking for more Madeira, asking his host to play the guitar, and Yusupov playing for two hours while the others wait upstairs for a poison to work.
stops.quote: The Madeira's good...give me some more.
stops.quote_source: Rasputin, in Prince Felix Yusupov, Lost Splendor, ch. XXIII, the murderer's account of the night of 16-17 December 1916 Old Style
suggested_refs: Roger W. Byard, 'The Death of Grigori Rasputin: A Forensic Evaluation', Forensic Science, Medicine and Pathology (2024)
sources: Felix Yusupov, Lost Splendor, ch. XXIII

stops.name: Petrograd, the courtyard of the Moika Palace
stops.date_confidence: Attested that shots were heard, that police attended, and that blood and other traces contradicted the conspirators' first story; the account is Yusupov's own. No public murder trial was ever held. New Style date; 17 December 1916 Old Style. The dog killed in the yard is standard in the literature on the night and is not separately verified here.
stops.campa: A policeman on the Moika hears shots in the small hours and comes to the door. The conspirators tell him a dog was killed in the yard, and there is a dog in the yard, killed for the purpose. It does not hold. There is blood on the snow and on the stairs, and by morning the city knows, and by the second day the Tsaritsa knows. Nobody is ever tried. Yusupov is sent by imperial order to his estate in Kursk province and Grand Duke Dmitri to the Persian front.
suggested_refs: The absence of any murder trial; the conspirators exiled by imperial order rather than prosecuted
sources: Felix Yusupov, Lost Splendor, ch. XXIII, alexanderpalace.org/lostsplendor/XXIII.html

stops.name: Petrograd, the Bolshoy Petrovsky Bridge
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The body was driven to the Bolshoy Petrovsky Bridge over the Malaya Nevka and put through the ice; en.wikipedia records its recovery about two hundred metres downstream, on 1 January 1917 New Style. Coordinates corrected to the bridge itself (59.9648944, 30.2547472); the research pool's earlier pin lay about 1.4 kilometres east, off the bridge. Byard 2024 finds no persuasive evidence of drowning, the head wound being immediately fatal and inflicted before immersion; the image of a living man clawing at the ice is later folklore.
stops.campa: They wrap him in a curtain, tie him, drive out to the islands, and put him through a hole in the ice of the Malaya Nevka in the dark. He is brought up two days later, about two hundred metres downstream. The legend says he was alive under the ice, that his lungs held water, that one arm was raised as if to bless. A forensic pathologist reading the postmortem photographs in 2024 found a contact wound in the middle of the forehead with the muzzle's own mark burned around it, and concluded that the head wound killed him before the water could.
suggested_refs: The postmortem photographs of 1917, the only surviving forensic record, the autopsy report itself being lost

segments.name: The Body and What Was Made of It

stops.name: Tsarskoye Selo, the chapel under construction
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the burial, corrected as to the date. The burial took place on 21 December 1916 Old Style; with the thirteen-day offset that is 3 January 1917 New Style. Wikipedia's '2 January' is an arithmetic slip rather than a competing tradition, and the research pool carried both readings; they are reconciled here in favour of 3 January. Coordinates are an approximate placement near Alexander Park, since no source pinpointing Anna Vyrubova's chapel site was located. His wife, his mistresses and his children were excluded from the funeral.
stops.campa: He is buried in the frozen ground beside a chapel Anna Vyrubova is having built on her land at Tsarskoye Selo, before dawn, with the Tsar and Tsaritsa and the four grand duchesses present and almost nobody else. His wife is not there. His children are not there. Alexandra puts an icon into the coffin, signed on the back by herself and her daughters, and a letter of her own. Nine weeks later the dynasty that buried him in secret will no longer exist.
suggested_refs: The unfinished chapel on Anna Vyrubova's property at Tsarskoye Selo

stops.name: Near Petrograd, the fire
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the exhumation and burning, unresolved as to the place. Soldiers acting on Alexander Kerensky's orders exhumed the body in March 1917 to stop the grave becoming a monarchist rallying point, transported it toward Petrograd, and burned it; sources conflict on the exact site, on whether the vehicle broke down en route, and on the fate of the ashes. The coordinates are a rough placement in the Lesnoye area outside Petrograd and are the weakest-grounded in this file. Day unknown, defaulted to 01. The story of the corpse sitting up in the flames is circulating folklore with no contemporary source located.
stops.campa: The revolution digs him up. Soldiers open the grave, load the coffin, drive toward Petrograd, and burn the body in the open somewhere along the way, because a grave visited by monarchists is a problem and ashes are not. Where exactly, whether the lorry broke down on the road, and what became of the ashes afterwards: the sources do not agree on any of it, and the site pinned here is the least certain in his whole itinerary. The story that the corpse sat up in the fire is repeated everywhere and rests on nothing. There is no grave.
suggested_refs: Alexander Kerensky's exhumation order, March 1917
sources: Research dossier, which flags the site as disputed

stops.name: Pokrovskoye, the house pulled down
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Ru.wikipedia's article on the G. E. Rasputin Museum records the original house as dismantled on the eve of the 1980 Olympics; a Tyumen regional bibliographic index attributes the demolition to regional Communist Party officials as deliberate erasure. The museum founded in 1990 by Vladimir and Marina Smirnov stands at Sovetskaya Street 78, in a different house across the road from where Rasputin's stood, and its coordinates are used here (57.240391, 66.791346), replacing a pool pin about fifty-six kilometres north. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Sixty-four years after he last walked out of it, the house in Pokrovskoye is taken down by order of the regional party, on the eve of the Moscow Olympics, because foreigners will be in the country and there is to be nothing here to see. The village keeps the story anyway. In 1990 a couple named Smirnov open a museum in a house across the road, the first in Russia devoted to him, and fill it with what they can find. Visitors come. Some of them bring icons of him, painted with no church's permission.
suggested_refs: The G. E. Rasputin Museum, Sovetskaya Street 78, Pokrovskoye, founded 1990 by Vladimir and Marina Smirnov
sources: writer-tyumen.ru, regional bibliographic index of Tyumen publications on Rasputin
The Moscow Times, 'Orthodox Church Takes on Rasputin' (for the icon-venerating movement)

stops.name: St Petersburg, apartment 20 as it stands
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the museum's existence and contents, undated as to its founding. The apartment museum's own site records the flat he rented from May 1914 and left for the last time on the night of the murder, and describes layers of wallpaper dated to successive decades from 1905, pre-revolutionary journals and documents, and period furnishings; it gives no opening date, so 1990-01-01 is a placement only. Coordinates are the corrected 64 Gorokhovaya fix, identical to the tenancy stop, replacing a pool pin about a kilometre off.
stops.campa: The flat is still there, up the same staircase, and it is shown by appointment. The walls have been opened to their layers: paper from 1905, paper from the twenties, paper from later, one over the other in the rooms where the petitioners queued. Downstairs is the street he walked out of after midnight to get into Yusupov's car. A disco record made him Russia's greatest love machine in 1978. The church that acquitted him twice has twice been asked to make him a saint and has twice refused. Visitors ring the bell and are let in.
suggested_refs: Patriarch Alexy II, December 2001, rejecting the canonization campaign: a church that equally venerates murderers and martyrs, lechers and saints
Boney M, 'Rasputin' (1978), and its 2021 resurgence
Antony Beevor, Rasputin: The Downfall of the Romanovs (Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 2026)
sources: The Moscow Times, 'Orthodox Church Takes on Rasputin' (5 February 2003, quoting the Patriarch's December 2001 denunciation)
